title: Judgement, the Bridge, and Repentance
setting: Heaven, the garden at evening, the gates of Hell and Chaos, Pandemonium, then Eden through a cold and stormy night
summary: The Son comes down to judge Adam, Eve and the serpent, tempering justice with mercy, and clothes the fallen pair. Sin and Death build a bridge from Hell to the world, and Satan returns to Pandemonium in triumph, only to be turned with all his followers into hissing serpents. On a ruined earth Adam despairs and rejects Eve, but her humble plea reconciles them, and together they turn to prayer.

sections.title: The news reaches Heaven
sections.note: The angel guards fly up from Paradise, sad and puzzled at how Satan got in. Heaven grieves, but with a pity that does not break its bliss.

sections.title: The Father sends the Son to judge
sections.note: God clears the guards of blame and insists his foreknowledge did not force the Fall. He sends the Son as judge, and the Son accepts, promising to temper justice with mercy and to take the worst on himself.

sections.title: The questioning in the garden
sections.note: In the cool of the evening the Son calls ‘Where art thou, Adam?’ Adam, cornered, blames ‘this Woman whom thou madest’; the Son rebukes him for making her his guide, and Eve answers simply, ‘The Serpent me beguiled.’

sections.title: The sentences
sections.note: The Son curses the serpent, then Eve, then Adam, in words taken almost directly from Genesis 3. Milton pauses to explain that the curse on the serpent’s head points to Christ’s final victory over Satan.

sections.title: The Son clothes them
sections.note: Like a father, and like a servant washing feet, the Son clothes their nakedness with skins, and their inner nakedness with his righteousness. He returns to Heaven and intercedes for them.

sections.title: Sin and Death build the bridge
sections.note: At Hell’s open gate Sin feels a new pull toward the world, and Death scents carnage there. Together they pile up the matter of Chaos into a huge causeway from Hell to the outside of the universe.

sections.title: Satan meets his children
sections.note: Satan, returning disguised as an angel, meets Sin and Death at the bridge. Sin praises him as its true architect, and he sends them down to rule the earth and make Man first their slave, then their prey.

sections.title: Satan’s triumph in Pandemonium
sections.note: Satan slips through deserted Hell disguised as a common soldier, then appears in blazing glory on his throne. He boasts that he has won a whole world from God ‘with an apple.’

sections.title: The great hiss
sections.note: Instead of applause Satan hears a universal hiss, and finds himself and all his followers turned into serpents. A grove of fruit like the forbidden tree springs up, and they chew it only to taste ashes.

sections.title: Sin and Death in Paradise
sections.note: Sin and Death arrive on earth and plan their feast. God tells the angels he has let these ‘Hell-hounds’ in to lick up the filth of sin, until the Son seals them in Hell for ever.

sections.title: The angels change the world
sections.note: The angels sing God’s justice, then set about altering the heavens: seasons, harsh winds and malign planetary influences begin. Discord enters the animals, and beast turns on beast.

sections.title: Adam’s night of despair
sections.note: Lying on the cold ground, Adam laments that all his children will curse him and argues with God and with himself. He ends by taking all the blame and crying out to his own conscience.

sections.title: Adam spurns Eve; her plea
sections.note: Adam calls Eve ‘thou Serpent’ and rails against the creation of woman. Eve falls at his feet, begs for peace between them, and offers to ask that the whole sentence fall on her alone.

sections.title: Reconciliation, and Eve’s desperate counsel
sections.note: Adam’s anger melts and he raises her. Eve, wanting to spare their unborn children, proposes that they stay childless or end their own lives.

sections.title: Adam’s counsel and their repentance
sections.note: Adam refuses despair: the promise that her seed will crush the serpent gives hope, and God judged them gently. He proposes they return to the place of judgement and pray, and the book ends as they do it, in almost the same words.

glosses.note: Deputy, one who rules on another’s behalf.
Side by side, equal: the Son sits at the Father’s right hand.
Jesus’ words in Luke 10:18: ‘I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.’
Satan’s title in Ephesians 2:2.
From Psalm 68 and Ephesians 4:8, read as Christ’s triumph over sin and death at his ascension.
The skin a snake sheds; Milton allows that the skins God used may have been shed rather than taken from slain beasts.
Form or shape: Death, who has no proper shape.
Keen-scented, in its old literal sense.
The Arctic Ocean.
The Pechora region of northern Russia, beyond which explorers hoped to find a northeast passage to China (Cathay).
Turning things to stone.
The Greek island that floated loose until Zeus fixed it so Latona could give birth there.
Like the Gorgon Medusa, whose look turned people to stone.
A massive pier or causeway of stone.
The Persian king who bridged the Hellespont with boats to invade Greece, and had the sea whipped when a storm broke his bridge.
Bridge-building (from Latin pons, bridge), with a dig at the pope, the Pontifex.

glosses.word: Betwixt the Centaur and the Scorpion
glosses.note: Satan steers through Sagittarius and Scorpio, far across the sky from Aries, where the sun is rising, to avoid being seen.
Square shape; Heaven is imagined as square, the created world as round (‘orbicular’).
Causeway.
Astrakhan on the Volga. The simile pictures Tartars retreating before the Russians and the Persian shah (‘Bactrin Sophi’) retreating before the Turks.
A council of state, from the Turkish word.
A fabled serpent with a head at each end. This catalogue of snakes comes from the Roman poet Lucan, who told how they sprang from the Gorgon’s blood in Libya.
The huge serpent bred from the mud after the flood and slain by Apollo at Delphi.
One of the Furies, who had snakes for hair.
Fruit near the Dead Sea was said to look ripe but turn to ash and smoke when bitten.
In a Greek myth, the serpent Ophion and Eurynome ruled Olympus before Saturn; Milton suggests the devils spread a garbled memory of the serpent and Eve.
Death rides a pale horse in Revelation 6:8.
Astrological aspects, the angles of 60, 90 and 120 degrees between planets, thought to shape their influence on earth.
Aslant. One theory has the angels tilt the earth’s axis by more than twenty degrees, creating the seasons.
The Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, in Taurus; the ‘Spartan Twins’ are Castor and Pollux, the constellation Gemini.
The sun turned back in horror when Atreus served Thyestes the flesh of his own sons.
Kindle, set alight.

famous.why: Satan waits for applause and gets ‘a dismal universal hiss’: the poem’s great comic reversal.
‘O miserable of happy!’ opens Adam’s long, searching lament, the first full portrait of a guilty conscience.
‘Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me Man?’ Mary Shelley used these lines as the epigraph to Frankenstein.
Adam’s cry to his conscience sums up his despair before Eve’s intervention.
Eve’s confession, ‘thou against God only; I against God and thee,’ begins the human work of reconciliation.
The narrator repeats Adam’s proposal almost word for word as the pair carry it out, a quiet and moving close.

themes: Justice and mercy meet in the Son, who judges and clothes the fallen in the same visit.
Evil’s triumphs turn into self-punishment: Satan is made the serpent he used.
Sin changes the whole world, from the tilt of the earth to the war among animals.
Reconciliation begins with a human act, Eve’s humble plea, before any word from Heaven.
art: Satan on his throne in Pandemonium, arms clinging to his ribs as he collapses into a vast serpent, while the hall around him writhes with hissing snakes.
